title: QBR Healthscore Metric Specs & Renewal Tracker Worksheet (draft)
content:
Purpose:
This document is a living draft for the Customer Success QBR metric definitions and a lightweight renewal tracker worksheet. Use it when preparing QBRs to ensure consistent definitions between CS, SRE, and Solutions Eng, and to provide quick recommended actions tied to metric thresholds.

Scope:
- Core metric definitions: latency (p50/p95/p99), uptime, cost/token, cache hit rate.
- Measurement windows and canonical data sources.
- Per-customer KPI template and sample rows for the renewal tracker.
- Recommended actions and short playbook pointers for common failure modes.

Quick note: this is intentionally pragmatic — we prioritize metrics that are computable from Redwood Console telemetry plus billing exports. Keep the definitions executable (i.e., everyone should be able to reproduce numbers from the console dashboards).

Measurement windows & data sources:
- Primary window for QBRs: trailing 90 days (default). Use trailing 30 days for more recent changes and trailing 7 days for immediate incidents called out in the QBR.
- Canonical sources:
  - Redwood Console per-route metrics (latency histograms, counts, cache stats)
  - Billing exports (daily CSV) for monetary spend and token counts
  - Tracing/Spans (Datadog/OTel) for request-level latency attribution (if customer has tracing enabled)
- Sampling considerations: for high-volume customers we may sample requests for per-request traces, but aggregated histograms in Console should be the source of record.

Metric definitions (canonical):
1) Latency (interactive inference)
   - What we report: p50, p95, p99 for final-token latency (ms).
   - Formula: compute latency per request from first-server-receive to final-token-emitted. Aggregate across the chosen window.
   - Scope: measured at route/model level; for streaming endpoints use the latency to first token and to final token separately.
   - Notes: For multi-stage flows (tool-calls, function-calling), report overall end-to-end latency and annotate breakdown (model time vs orchestration time).
   - Typical green/yellow/red thresholds (example): p95 < 400ms (green), 400-900ms (yellow), >900ms (red). Adjust per route SLA.

2) Uptime (availability)
   - What we report: percent of requests that returned a 2xx or expected application-level response within the SLA window.
   - Formula: (successful_requests_within_slo / total_requests) * 100 over the measurement window.
   - Counting: successful_requests excludes client-side validation errors (4xx) unless the customer’s integration indicates mis-configuration. Time-based outages should be measured with 1-minute resolution.
   - Inclusion: micro-degradations (e.g., elevated latency but still returning responses) are not counted as failures for uptime but should appear in latency and error-rate metrics.
   - SLO example: 99.9% over 90 days for enterprise customers (configurable per contract).

3) Cost per token (unit economics)
   - What we report: USD per 1k tokens (or per 1M tokens depending on scale).
   - Formula (simple): (inference_spend_for_window / total_output_tokens_for_window) * 1000 => USD per 1k tokens.
   - Notes: decide whether to include input tokens in denominator (we recommend reporting both: cost_per_output_token and cost_per_total_token). Billing export contains spend; token counts come from Console export.
   - Granularity: calculate per-model and per-route. Also report weighted average for the customer.
   - Example thresholds: <$0.50 per 1k tokens (green for some open models), $0.50-$2.00 (yellow), >$2.00 (red) — these are examples; actual targets vary by model family and reserved capacity terms.

4) Cache hit rate (prefix/KV/result caching)
   - What we report: percent of cacheable requests that served from cache (hit) vs required model execution (miss).
   - Formula: (cache_hits / cacheable_requests) * 100 over the window.
   - Defining cacheable_requests: requests where caching policy allowed lookup (e.g., identical prompt hash, same model & routing policy, TTL not expired).
   - Additional clarifications: distinguish KV-cache (internal LM KV cache for autoregressive context) vs result cache (full-response caching). Report both if available.
   - Operational note: high cache-hit rate reduces cost/token and tail-latency; but watch for staleness (stale outputs depending on freshness requirements).

Other useful metrics (secondary):
- Error rate: 5xx / total_requests.
- Model fallback rate: fraction of requests routed from primary model to fallback.
- Cold-start rate: percent of requests that experienced GPU start-up beyond expected baseline.
- Latency breakdown: orchestration vs model vs network (from traces).

KPI table template (pasteable into Google Sheet or use directly in QBR slide):
Columns: Metric | Window | Route/Model | Value | Target | Delta vs previous window | Owner | Notes
Sample rows (text):
- Latency p95 | 90d | /gen-chat-v1 | 420ms | <400ms | +60ms vs 90d prior | eng-sre | streaming first-token=120ms
- Uptime % | 90d | account-1234 (prod) | 99.92% | >=99.9% | -0.02% | cs | one incident 2026-01-09 (JIRA-CCS-987)
- Cost per 1k tokens | 90d | model-mosaic-3b | $0.78 | <$0.60 | +$0.18 | finance | high token churn from interactive sessions
- Cache hit rate | 90d | /search-rank | 64% | >70% | -6pp | solutions-eng | TTL short (30s) leading to misses

Healthscore (composite) suggestion:
- Simple weighted model for QBRs: 40% latency, 30% uptime, 20% cost/token, 10% cache hit. Normalize each metric to 0-100 then compute weighted average.
- Example mapping: latency green=>100, yellow=>60, red=>20. Keep this mapping in the QBR slide notes (customers will want transparency on how healthscore was computed).

Playbook snippets (quick-action):
- If latency p95 > SLA and p99 spikes:
  1) Check per-route batch size and concurrency in Console.
  2) Check KV cache effectiveness and prefix cache settings.
  3) If model CPU/GPU saturation: escalate to infra (tag eng-infra) and propose short-term dedicated capacity or reserve burst.
  4) Run quick eval on a sample prompt set to identify regressions in token count or model runtime.

- If cost per token increased >20% vs prior quarter:
  1) Check model mix changes (new model routed in can increase cost).
  2) Recommend batching adjustments, token trimming, or cheaper-compatible model variant for non-critical routes.
  3) Solutions Eng to propose conservative quantization or dynamic routing policy.

- If cache hit rate < target:
  1) Verify TTLs and cache key definitions (hashing of prompt variables).
  2) Work with customer to identify stable prefixes that can be cached.
  3) Consider result-caching for high-traffic static prompts.

Renewal tracker worksheet (lightweight columns for QBR):
Columns: Customer | ARR (USD) | Next renewal | QBR date | Healthscore (0-100) | Key metric callouts | Action items | Renewal recommendation
Sample rows (text):
- Acme Corp | $480k | 2026-05-15 | 78 | p95 latency slightly above target; cache 58% | Increase TTL on search route; plan canary of dedicated-pool | Recommend renewal at current commit with 10% uplift for Dedicated pilot
- Nimbus Retail | $120k | 2026-04-10 | 92 | Stable latency and uptime; cost optimized | Offer 12-month reserved discount to lock pricing | Target expansion of embeddings workload
